transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-27
Start: 11:32 AM UTC
Duration: ~74 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SA); Dana Morris (CTO - Seacliff), Elena Ruiz (Head of Security), Marcus Lee (Cloud Infra), Priya Nair (DevOps), Omar Haddad (Procurement)

Summary (auto):
Customer wants a deep dive on Private/VPC deployment security: network isolation, ingress/egress patterns, firewalling, KMS/customer-managed keys, audit log forwarding and SOC2/ISO controls; evaluate feasibility for air-gapped / on-prem option and pilot timeline.

Topics: network design, VPC peering vs Transit Gateway, private endpoints, egress control, bastion/NAT, firewall rules, RBAC/SSO integration, KMS/CMEK, audit logs/SIEM integration, compliance artifacts.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Cole: Hey everyone thanks for joining; we'll start with quick intros. I'm Avery, AE at Redwood, Riley and Samir are our engineering leads for private deployments.
[00:18] Dana Morris: Hi all, Dana here CTO. We're evaluating Redwood Private for sensitive PII workloads and want to understand network isolation and how you handle ingress/egress and keys.
[00:30] Riley Chen: Thanks Dana. Quick agenda - we'll walk through recommended VPC architecture for Private, ingress patterns (internal ALB or NLB), egress controls, key management options (customer-managed KMS, HSM), and logging/audit integration. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps.
[00:45] Elena Ruiz: I appreciate that. We have strict SOC 2 and ISO requirements. Also need SSO/SAML integration for RBAC and detailed audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:56] Samir Patel: Totally. We'll surface the controls you care about and map them to Redwood controls and the deployment responsibilities.
[01:05] Marcus Lee: Quick note - our infra is AWS us-west-2, we use TGW for multi-account connectivity and central logging to Splunk, and Okta for SSO. We prefer VPC peering for some legacy accounts but open to Transit Gateway.
[01:20] Riley Chen: Good context. For Private VPC we typically offer two deployment patterns: 1) Customer-managed VPC where Redwood deploys within your VPC (we call it customer-hosted), or 2) Redwood-managed VPC with VPC peering or private endpoint. Both support strict isolation.
[01:36] Dana Morris: Could you sketch the differences now?
[01:40] Riley Chen: Sure. In customer-managed VPC, Redwood furnishes AMI/container images that run inside your subnets - you control security groups, NACLs, route tables. We recommend placing inference nodes in private subnets with no public IPs, behind an internal NLB. Control plane connectivity to Redwood's management plane can be via a private peering or PrivateLink, or you can run an air-gapped control plane if you need.
[02:05] Priya Nair: Air-gapped meaning fully on-prem?
[02:08] Samir Patel: Yes, air-gapped or on-prem package - in that mode the control plane is entirely in-customer network; we ship the artifacts and assist with ops. That's a heavier integration and we treat that as an enterprise private deployment with extra audit support.
[02:22] Elena Ruiz: For our compliance we prefer the customer-managed VPC pattern so keys never leave our KMS. How does Redwood integrate with customer KMS?
[02:30] Riley Chen: We support CMEK - customer-managed encryption keys - via cross-account KMS grants or direct in-VPC HSM integrations depending on cloud. Typical pattern: data-at-rest uses envelope encryption; the root DEK is encrypted with your customer KMS key. Redwood services never persist plaintext keys. We can support AWS KMS customer keys, Cloud HSM for FIPS requirements, and rotation policies aligned with your governance.
[02:55] Marcus Lee: Cross-account KMS grants - any gotchas there?
[02:58] Samir Patel: Need to set key policy to allow Redwood's service principal or a specific IAM role in your account to decrypt. We provide an example IAM role and key policy template. Also suggest a least-privilege approach and monitoring of key usage via CloudTrail.
[03:15] Dana Morris: Good. What about ingress - how do clients talk to the model endpoints without exposing public IPs?
[03:20] Riley Chen: Options: internal NLB (private), AWS PrivateLink endpoints, or VPC peering with route controls. For multi-account setups Transit Gateway + route table isolations work well. In internal NLB pattern, the app traffic routes within your VPC to the inference nodes; you control ingress via security groups and ALB WAF if needed.
[03:41] Elena Ruiz: And egress? We need to lock down outbound to only specific services (S3 buckets, KMS endpoints, Redwood control plane IPs).
[03:48] Riley Chen: We recommend NAT gateways with explicit proxying for permitted hosts, or egress-only via a firewall appliance (we've integrated with Palo Alto/Checkpoint in other deployments). For S3 access can use VPC endpoints (gateway endpoints) and restrict S3 bucket policies to only the VPC. For KMS, calls go to the regional KMS endpoint; if you require, you can use VPC endpoints for KMS (PrivateLink) or route via a proxy so the calls never traverse internet.
[04:12] Marcus Lee: Concern: you said Redwood control plane may need connectivity - can we allow only a small set of IP ranges?
[04:17] Samir Patel: Yes, we publish a set of static egress IP ranges for our management plane. For customer-managed VPC with peering, we can avoid public egress by using PrivateLink/peering. Where external connectivity is required we can support dedicated egress IPs and mutual TLS for control plane authentication.
[04:33] Priya Nair: How are firewall rules handled? We use strict NACLs and host-based firewalls too.
[04:38] Riley Chen: You own the security groups and NACLs. We provide recommended templates that lock ports to only the internal load balancer and management roles. For host firewalling we recommend restricting outbound to only KMS, S3, logging endpoints and your SIEM; block all else.
[04:52] Elena Ruiz: Audit logs - we need full request logs for governance and to forward them to Splunk with 7 years retention. How does Redwood produce logs?
[05:00] Samir Patel: We emit detailed audit events: API calls, inference request metadata (no sensitive request payload unless configured), model version, request timestamps, authentication context (user/service account). We support forwarding to your Splunk via HTTPS or syslog collector; we can integrate with our Fluentd/Vector agents to push logs into your central account or into a Redshift/S3 bucket under your control. Retention is a customer setting if logs are in your account. If logs are in Redwood-managed storage we can support export and retention SLAs via contract.
[05:28] Dana Morris: When you say 'no sensitive payloads', can we ensure that model inputs are not stored?
[05:33] Riley Chen: Yes - for regulated workloads we have a configuration flag to disable request body persistence in storage and logs. We still emit metadata for observability but avoid storing full prompts. If you want full isolation, run in customer-managed VPC and direct logs to your SIEM.
[05:47] Elena Ruiz: RBAC and SSO - we use Okta and SCIM to provision users.
[05:52] Samir Patel: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. For Private we support SAML identity provider integration and map assertions to RBAC roles. We also support service-account style credentials tied to IAM roles so infra automation can authenticate without human SSO.
[06:08] Marcus Lee: Any options for mTLS between our app and the inference endpoints?
[06:11] Riley Chen: Yes - we support mutual TLS for in-VPC endpoints. You can manage certs in your cert manager and configure the NLB/TLS listener to require client certs.
[06:22] Priya Nair: What about network latency - adding private link/proxy will add hops. Any data on added latency?
[06:27] Samir Patel: Minimal, usually sub-5ms additional in-region for PrivateLink. We can run benchmarks in your environment as part of the pilot - that's a recommended step.
[06:37] Elena Ruiz: From a compliance perspective we need SOC 2 controls mapping and proof of encryption in transit and at rest.
[06:44] Avery Cole: We'll share our SOC 2 Type II report and an architecture controls mapping doc that maps Redwood controls to the Trust Services Criteria; we'll also include our encryption in transit details (TLS 1.3, mTLS options) and key management docs.
[06:57] Dana Morris: Are you ISO 27001 certified?
[07:00] Avery Cole: We have ISO docs in progress - we maintain a security program aligned with ISO 27001; I'll include the current attestation paperwork.
[07:08] Marcus Lee: Pen test - do you allow customers to run blackbox pen tests against private deployments?
[07:13] Samir Patel: For customer-managed VPC, you own the perimeter and can do pen tests. For Redwood-managed components, we coordinate and there is an approval workflow. We also provide our own third-party pen test reports on request.
[07:27] Elena Ruiz: Data residency - we require all processing to stay within us-west-2.
[07:31] Riley Chen: We can pin compute to a single region for the Private deployment. Our scheduler supports region pinning and we can disable cross-region failover for the pilot to satisfy residency.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Backup and snapshots - who controls them?
[07:44] Samir Patel: For customer-managed VPC, backups (EBS snapshots, S3 backups) can be in your account under your control; we recommend encrypted snapshots and bucket policies that restrict access. For Redwood-managed storage we can arrange exportable encrypted backups and retention controls per contract.
[07:59] Dana Morris: Could you walk through a sample network diagram quickly?
[08:03] Riley Chen: Sure - high level: your transit gateway connects accounts -> customer VPC hosting Redwood inference nodes in private subnets -> internal NLB in private subnet -> app VPC/ENIs route to NLB. Management plane either peered via PrivateLink to our management account or run as a customer-controlled control plane. Logging agent (Fluentd/Vector) forwards logs to your Splunk collector - either to an internal HTTP endpoint or to S3. KMS is customer key with cross-account grant to our service role.
[08:31] Marcus Lee: For firewalling we want explicit deny-by-default, allow only ports 443 between app and NLB and port 22 only to bastion with MFA.
[08:40] Riley Chen: That's exactly the template we provide. We also recommend host-based agents for EDR and enabling connection monitoring.
[08:49] Elena Ruiz: About auditability - can we get immutable logs with signature?
[08:53] Samir Patel: If logs are stored in your S3 bucket, you can enable object locking to meet immutability needs and use CloudTrail + KMS logs for signature and verification. We can also forward to your SIEM with signed events.
[09:06] Priya Nair: One more - how do you handle model artifacts (weights)? We need to ensure model files are encrypted and access controlled.
[09:12] Riley Chen: Model weights are stored encrypted at rest. In customer-managed setups, weights can be stored in your S3 and mounted with appropriate IAM policies. For Redwood-managed storage we enforce envelope encryption with KMS and restrict access to the inference service role only.
[09:27] Dana Morris: Procurement question - what is typical pilot length and cost?
[09:31] Avery Cole: Typically 4\u20136 weeks for a pilot with a small cluster; we provide a pricing estimate for dedicated pilot capacity and include some professional services hours for onboarding. We'll send a formal pilot SOW after this call.
[09:43] Omar Haddad: On contract terms we need indemnities and SOC attestation clauses.
[09:47] Avery Cole: Understood - we'll include SOC attachment and standard SLAs; procurement will get the legal packet.
[09:54] Riley Chen: Any other technical questions?
[09:57] Marcus Lee: A couple of specifics: 1) Can you support private S3 access without NAT? 2) How do you handle cross-account IAM for ephemeral inference roles?
[10:05] Samir Patel: 1) Yes use S3 gateway endpoints and bucket policies scoped to VPC endpoints. 2) We use short-lived credentials via a workload identity approach - assume-role with STS and limited session duration; we supply example IAM trust policies and role names.
[10:20] Elena Ruiz: Do you have SOC controls for personnel access and background checks?
[10:24] Avery Cole: Yes, personnel controls are part of SOC 2; we can share high-level HR control summaries in the package.
[10:31] Dana Morris: Great. I'd like a security workshop next week to review the VPC diagram with our infra team.
[10:36] Samir Patel: We'll set that up - Samir will run the workshop and bring an infra deep-dive deck.
[10:41] Avery Cole: Recap of next steps - we'll send SOC2/ISO docs, a sample VPC diagram, and pilot SOW. Marcus will share CIDRs and egress list. We'll schedule the workshop.
[10:52] Priya Nair: Minor transcription note - earlier you mentioned KV cache, I heard K V cake which made everyone hungry -
[10:58] Riley Chen: [laughs] yes KV cache, not cake.
[11:02] Dana Morris: Thanks everyone - this was helpful.
[11:05] Avery Cole: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and invite for the workshop.

End of meeting.
